reason: Peristome teeth curve inward (incurved) in mosses. The examples are correct.
The bearer is the sporocarp (a fern part). Its outline seen from the side is a 2-D shape, and the examples are shapes.
A mericarp can be narrowed gradually to its apex or base. The examples are correct.

Epigeal and hypogeal describe how germination goes (cotyledons above or below ground). They do not describe where the seedling is. A rule would map epigeal/hypogeal to value terms and put the cotyledon, not the seedling, as the bearer.
The syconium ostiole (the opening of a fig) can be open or closed.
The height of a drupe is a real measurement. The examples are correct, although they sit close to length.
A pinna rachis can be hairy (puberulent and similar). The examples are correct.
Legume fruits (pods) can be ascending in orientation. The examples come from one flora and the plural might refer to valves or hairs, so I'm only fairly sure.
Berries can be hairy or glabrescent. The examples are correct.
An orchid labellum can be funnel-shaped.
A cymbiform or boat-shaped labellum is the same as scaphoid. This is a standard orchid term.

Most examples are measured widths ('larges de 4–6 mm'), and a measurement is not 'increased'. Only 'élargies' truly means increased width. A rule would send measurements to plain width and keep this pair for explicit words such as broadened or widened.
A domatium can be small. The examples are correct.

'Orné' (ornamented) on its own says nothing. The examples are really a colour spot, ridges and grooves. A rule would need to turn the named feature (crest, groove, spot) into its own part or quality, and keep 'ornamented' only when nothing more is said.
Ornamentation is a noun for a structure, not a quality. The examples (folds, rows of papillae, a crest) are parts or textures that should be annotated for what they are.
Short, head-like spikes can be orbicular, but the French 'orbiculaires' examples may describe bracts or glumes instead. A rule would need the bearer word in the same clause.
The examples ('basal auricles rounded', 'apex rounded', 'base rounded') do not describe trichomes. The pair comes from the wrong part.
Pitchers are leaves, and a pitcher can be nearly cylindrical. The examples are correct.
A foveolate (pitted) areole fits cacti and similar plants, but areole is mapped here to 'areole bud'. A rule would need areole to be its own part, or the pits to be treated as a surface feature.
The syconium ostiole can be closed.
A plant ovary can be lobed (for example 6-lobed).
A stipel can be conical.
All examples are measured widths ('5-7 mm wide'). The quality should be plain width, not 'increased width'. That is a wrong reading of the value.
A calyx with parallel ribs (striate-nerved) has parallel venation. The examples are correct.
Xylem vessels have a measurable diameter. The examples are pore diameters.
A thallus can be spotted (maculate).
The third number of a length × width × depth triple is the depth (thickness) of the mericarp.
An achene, or its beak, can be straight.
In the examples 'continuous' describes the glands ('glands rarely continuous'), not the fruit. The pair comes from the wrong part.
'Withering in fruit' is about petals persisting or falling, which is closer to persistence than to a shrivelled shape. A rule would need to separate wilting after flowering from persistence.
Ephemeral leaves are short-lived leaves. This matches decreased life span.
Mericarps can be constricted (between the seeds). The examples are correct.
The length of an epicalyx segment, here stated relative to the sepals, is a valid quality.
A palea can be spatulate.
Achenes with a feathery beak or pappus are called plumose. The examples are correct.
Petals can be cream-coloured.
Stems can be cane-like or wand-like.
The colour of the outer (abaxial) side of a tepal is valid.
A corolla lip can be warty (verrucose).
An awn can be spinulose, meaning it has small spines.
The leaf collar (a grass part) can be present or absent. Several examples are other collars ('chalazal collar', 'involucral collars'). A rule would need to keep only collars of leaves or sheaths.
A capsule, or its apex, can be acuminate.
A rostellum (an orchid part) can be present or absent.
The summit (mouth) of a leaf sheath can be U-shaped.
Old leaf sheaths can be fibrillose, with fine fibres.
Spikes can be suberect, meaning nearly erect.
A leaf margin or border can be narrow.
Short shoots can be erect. Some examples are about spurs, but they are the same kind of part.
A pinnule can be hairy or glabrous, including on one side only.
Branches can be weak. The examples are correct.

'Variable in shape and size' describes variation between bracts, not a quality of one bract. PATO variant means something else (differing from the standard). A rule should route 'variable' to the named attribute, such as shape or size.
'Unequal', 'subequal' and 'reduced' often describe awn branches or compare several awns, not the size of one awn. A rule would need to know what is being compared.
The inner (adaxial) surface of a sepal can be hairy.
The length of a leaf spine is a valid measurement.
'Ensiform' means sword-shaped. 'Blade-like' is a different PATO meaning, so this is a wrong reading. Use a shape term for ensiform instead.
The colour of flesh (storage tissue) is a valid quality.
A petiole can be suberect.
An indusium can be vaulted or arched.
In the examples the pits are bowl-shaped, not the seed. A rule would need to treat seed surface pits (crateriform sculpture) as a separate part or a seed surface texture.
The axis of a higher-order inflorescence, often its apex, can be ciliate.
